verses.translation_literal: A psalm, a song of the dedication of the house, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm. A song for the day the house was dedicated, and the song is David's.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a title, but it is the first thing the performers see, and it tells them the occasion: the opening of a house. Which house is the first puzzle, because the psalm itself never mentions one. Rashi and Metzudat David take it for the Temple, with the Levites singing it at its dedication; Ibn Ezra prefers David's own cedar palace; Malbim reads the house as the body, rebuilt after sickness. Keep the ambiguity alive: the singers can play it as a feast of stone and cedar or as a man's own recovered frame.

The KJV's 'A Psalm and Song at the dedication of the house of David' is misleading in English, since it makes David the owner of the house; the Hebrew has 'of David' hanging at the end of the whole title, after 'the house'. Note also that the KJV's numbering counts this line as verse 0, so every KJV verse number in this psalm is one less than the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'Dedication', the opening and first use of a building; the root means to initiate or train, and is the word behind Hanukkah. Metzudat Zion says the beginning of a thing destined to stand is called chanukh in biblical Hebrew.
A psalm: a piece sung with instrumental accompaniment; it shares its root with the command 'sing praises' in verse 5.

verses.translation_literal: I will exalt you, YHWH, for you have drawn me up, and have not let my enemies rejoice over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will raise you high, O LORD, for you raised me, drew me up like water from a deep well, and you did not hand my enemies their laughter over me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker opens with a vow of praise, and the ground of the vow is a rescue. The verb for 'drawn up' (dalah) is the verb for hauling a bucket from a well, so the image is of a man at the bottom of a shaft and a hand on the rope. The KJV's 'lifted up' is correct but loses the water and the depth, and sets up the contrast with verse 4, where the same life is brought up from Sheol.

There is a pair of lifting words here: the speaker will 'exalt' (aromimcha) the one who 'drew him up' (dilitani). The exchange is exact: he lifts God in praise because God lifted him. The enemies are the audience of the scene; the stakes are public. The old rabbis hear the enemies as those saying David's sin was unforgiven (Rashi, Radak); Malbim and Ibn Ezra hear plain gloating over a sickbed. Either way the point is that the enemies were denied their joy. 'Rejoice over me' follows Rashi's reading of the lamed as 'alay.

philological_notes.note: 'You drew me up', the verb is used of drawing water from a well (Exod 2:16, 19). Metzudat Zion links it to 'my eyes were lifted (dalu) to the heights' in Isaiah 38:14, so the sense of lifting is also attested.
'I will exalt you', cohortative-sounding vow of praise; the root means high, so it answers the 'drawing up' with a raising of his own.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH my God, I cried for help to you, and you healed me.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, my God, I cried out to you, I called for help, and you healed me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Short, plain and close: three beats, call, cry, cure. The cry is shiva', a word for a shout for help, not a polite prayer. The KJV 'I cried unto thee' flattens it a little; the verb carries the desperation of someone who has no one else to call.

The healing is the surprise. Rashi and Metzudat David hear in 'you healed me' the forgiveness of sin (citing Isaiah 6:10), so that sickness and guilt are one illness. Ibn Ezra and Malbim hear the opposite stress: the cry was to God alone, not to a physician; there was no salve and no healer. To an ancient audience, with a physician's art mixed with magic and the gods of Egypt and Canaan, this is a claim of exclusivity. Play the line as quiet gratitude, with the speaker still a little out of breath.

philological_notes.note: 'I cried for help': a shout for rescue by someone who cannot save himself, a stronger word than 'pray'. Ibn Ezra stresses that the cry was to God alone, and not to a physician.
'And you healed me': in Rashi and Metzudat David the healing is forgiveness of sin (compare Isaiah 6:10); in the plain sense it is the cure of sickness.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, you brought up my life from Sheol; you kept me alive from my going down [to the] pit.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, you hauled my soul up out of Sheol. You gave me back my breath and held me from the long stairway down to the pit.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has been to the edge of the world of the dead, and the verse says so in two matched halves: up from Sheol, kept alive from going down. For Israelites Sheol is not hell in the later sense: it is the silent underworld beneath the earth where all the dead gather, and the 'pit' (bor) is a synonym for it, like a cistern or grave shaft. The KJV 'grave' for Sheol is a softening: the Hebrew has the name of the underworld, not the hole in the ground. And 'my soul' for nefesh hides the plain sense: nefesh is the living throat and breath, the whole life, so 'brought up my life' is exactly what the speaker means.

Note the text's own wrinkle: the written text says miyordei, 'from those who go down', but it is read miyyeredi, 'from my going down'. Rashi and Radak both prefer the reading as an infinitive. Either way, the speaker is counted among the near-dead. Radak and the other classical commentators take the pit as Gehenna; the plain reading is that Sheol is the destination of any dying man.

philological_notes.note: Sheol, the underworld abode of the dead. The KJV 'grave' makes it a hole in the ground and loses the sense of a realm.

Ketiv miyordei, 'from those who go down' (a plural participle; compare Ps 28:1, 143:7); Qere miyyeredi, 'from my going down' (an infinitive). Rashi, Radak and Meiri take the Qere, and Radak compares 'instead of my pursuing good' (Ps 38:21).
'You gave me life, kept me alive': the piel is causative, a giving of life.

verses.translation_literal: Sing praise to YHWH, his faithful ones, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to the LORD, all you who are his faithful, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera turns. Until now the psalm was a private cry; now the speaker calls the congregation to sing, as a man who has been rescued summons his neighbors. The 'faithful ones' (chasidim) are those bound to God by loyalty (chesed), and the KJV's 'saints' loads the word with later church usage: these are covenant loyalists, not canonized holy men. Rashi hears an invitation to the faithful that God will also treat them well, even if they are suffering; Ibn Ezra hears that what befell David can befall them, and the same God will rescue them.

The oddest phrase is 'the remembrance of his holiness', which the KJV renders 'at the remembrance of his holiness' as if a time. The Hebrew has a lamed, 'to', and 'remembrance' (zeker) is the name by which God is invoked: Radak says his name is the remembrance of his holiness, since that is how we recall him, as his essence is unknown to us. The ASV 'holy memorial name' catches it. Two verbs for praise, zamer (to sing with music) and hodu (to give thanks, to confess), share their root with the 'psalm' of verse 1 and later the words for thanks in verse 10.

philological_notes.note: 'His faithful ones': people marked by chesed, loyal love. 'Saints' (KJV) is a later churchly sense.
'To the remembrance of his holiness'. Radak says 'remembrance' is equivalent to 'his name', for by his name we remember him, although we do not know his essence.

verses.translation_literal: For a moment is in his anger, life is in his favor; in the evening weeping lodges, and at the morning, a ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: For his anger is a moment; his favor is a lifetime. Weeping may come to stay the night, but at dawn there is singing.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm and its most quoted line, built as a double balance: anger against favor, moment against life; evening against morning, weeping against a ringing shout. The Hebrew is lean: 'a moment in his anger, life in his favor' has no verbs at all, and the KJV supplies 'endureth' and 'is'. The ASV's 'a life-time' is a gloss; chayyim is plain 'life'.

The second half personifies grief as a guest. The verb yalin means to spend the night, to lodge: weeping comes at dusk like a traveler seeking a bed, and at the morning something else is at the door, rinnah, a shrill cry of joy. There is a grammatical gap: weeping has no 'in' and joy has no 'at' of its own. Ibn Ezra and Meiri note the missing bet and compare 2 Kings 12:11 and 'is he found in the house of the LORD'. The KJV's 'may endure' also softens: the Hebrew simply says it lodges.

Time is concrete. In the ancient day the night was a threefold watch, and a long night of mourning was real. Radak and Malbim take the 'evening' and 'morning' as the span of the punishment, short against the life that follows.

philological_notes.note: 'Lodges, spends the night': weeping is imagined as an overnight guest; the same verb is used of a traveler who stays the night (Gen 19:2).
A ringing shout, a cry of joy or triumph, from a root of sound; KJV 'joy' loses the cry.
Literally 'in his nose', an idiom for anger, since the nostril flares and snorts; the same word as 'nose' (af).

verses.translation_literal: And I, I said in my ease, I will not be shaken for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, I said, when all was well with me, in my easy peace: I shall never be shaken.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker confesses. 'And I' is emphatic and set against God in the previous verse: he turns from what God does to what he himself said. The word shalvi, from shalu, is not 'prosperity' as in the KJV, but ease, the false calm of someone who has not yet been tested. The KJV's 'prosperity' suggests wealth; the Hebrew describes a state of mind, a quiet that does not expect trouble.

The speech itself is boastful: 'I will not be shaken for ever', with the same verb (mot) used of the earth that cannot be moved and of the righteous who is not moved. It is the pride of the healthy, as Ibn Ezra says, who think illness cannot come. Rashi hears the voice of a man who forgot that his standing was in God's hands; Radak hears a man confident that the evil impulse could never move him; Meiri that the trouble was given to bring ease. For the actor, let the line begin smoothly and end in a faint irony.

philological_notes.note: 'In my ease, my tranquility': a carefree security, 'prosperity' in KJV is too materialist. Compare Metzudat David: 'when I was at ease I said I would never fall'.
'I will be shaken, moved': the root is used of a foot that slips and of the earth that quakes; bal ('not') is a poetic negative.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, in your favor you made my mountain stand [in] strength; you hid your face, I was terrified.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, in your favor you set my mountain on its feet, and made it strong. Then you hid your face, and I was seized with terror.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to verse 7 is brutal and brief. The speaker had said 'I shall not be shaken'; now he says it was God's favor that held the mountain up, and the moment God hid his face, he was gripped by panic. The pivot is the shortest clause in the psalm: 'you hid your face, I was terrified.' Do not soften it: nibhal means seized by sudden dread, not mildly 'troubled' as in the KJV and ASV.

To hide the face is the biblical image for withdrawn favor: in a world where a king's face smiling is life and his turning away is danger, the withdrawn face of God is the end of safety. 'My mountain' is the crux of the verse. It is likely a picture of the speaker's secure position (a mountain does not move), but the commentators split: Radak says it is his intellect, Malbim his body, Meiri his soul, Ibn Ezra reports three grammatical readings. Keep the plain image and let the audience feel it.

philological_notes.note: 'To my mountain, strength': 'oz is either a second object ('you made my mountain stand in strength') or adverbial. Radak takes 'my mountain' as the intellect; Malbim as the body. The image is of a secure standing.
'Terrified, dismayed': a sudden shock, stronger than the KJV 'troubled'.
'You hid your face': the idiom for the withdrawal of favor; compare the Targum, which has the divine Presence (shekhinta) go up.

verses.translation_literal: To you, YHWH, I called out, and to my Lord I sought favor.
verses.translation_dramatic: To you, LORD, I cried out. To my Lord I pleaded for mercy.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now replays the crisis in the past tense. After the hidden face there is only one thing to do, and he does it: he calls. The two verbs are a pair: qara' (to call out) and hitchannen (to beg for favor, from the root of grace), and the two divine titles are a pair as well: YHWH, the personal name, then Adonai, 'my Lord'. The KJV in the packet prints both as 'Lord', and the YLT gives 'Jehovah' twice, so the contrast is lost. The ancient listener would hear the name and the title of a master.

Ibn Ezra hears a man who found nothing else to do but cry and plead; Malbim, that the prayer was for the sake of God's honor and not just for his own life, a thought taken up in the next verse. The word order puts 'to you' first in both halves: the address is the emphasis.

philological_notes.note: 'I begged for favor': the hithpael of the root of grace (chen), the speech of someone who has no claim and asks for a gift.
'My Lord': a title, set beside the name YHWH; a pair of names in parallel.

verses.translation_literal: What profit is in my blood, in my going down to the pit? Will dust give thanks to you? Will it declare your faithfulness?
verses.translation_dramatic: What do you gain from my blood, if I go down to the pit? Can dust give you thanks? Can dust tell of your faithfulness?
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the argument of the prayer, and it is bold: a dead man is no use to God. The speaker bargains, not with merit, but with God's own interest. In Israel's older view, the dead lie silent in the dust and no longer join in worship; the life that praises is the life that is lived. 'What profit' (betza') is commercial language, a gain, a margin; the KJV keeps it, but the force is the shopkeeper's question: what do you make from this?

'My blood' is the life itself (the Hebrew idea that the blood is the nefesh, Ibn Ezra and Radak), so 'in my blood' means 'in my death, in my life poured out'. Metzudat David reads 'when my blood is shed'. The first of the two rhetorical questions uses the verb of verse 5: 'give thanks' (hodah) repeats the hodu of 'give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness'. Dust cannot do that, nor can it 'declare' (higgid). The KJV 'thy truth' for 'amitt'cha' is acceptable, but the word is closer to faithfulness, reliability: God's steadiness, which is what the living report. Malbim: while I live I tell your truth, but in death, who will?

philological_notes.note: 'Profit, gain': the word of the market, as in 'what profit is there?' (Mal 3:14). Metzudat Zion glosses it as benefit and desire.
'In my blood': the blood stands for the life; Radak equates the blood with the soul, Metzudat David reads 'when my blood is spilled'.
'Pit': a synonym of Sheol and bor; YLT 'corruption' reflects an alternative derivation from the verb 'to decay'. My own reading is that the context favors the pit.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, YHWH, and show me favor; YHWH, be a helper to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear me, LORD, and be gracious. LORD, be my help.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer itself, in its barest form: two commands and a plea. After the long argument of the last verse the speaker drops all rhetoric and speaks in the imperative, the verbs of a man with no standing but need. 'Hear' (shema') is the first word; then 'show me favor' (chonneni), the same root as the begging in verse 9; and last 'be a helper to me', literally 'be a helper for me'. YHWH is named twice, the divine name standing in each half of the plea.

It is one of the shortest verses in the psalm. Let the silence on either side of it be as long as the verse. The KJV 'have mercy' is serviceable, though chanan is the root of 'grace' rather than 'mercy'; Radak says the speaker asked also that if his foot had slipped, God be his help and raise him and forgive him. Meiri reads the plea as one for the fullness of the soul.

philological_notes.note: 'Show me favor': the root of grace (chen); 'have mercy' (KJV) shifts it to a different word-family, rachamim.
'A helper': a participle, used as a title, from the same root as the noun 'ezer that names the woman in Genesis 2:18.

verses.translation_literal: You turned my wailing into dancing for me; you loosened my sackcloth, and girded me [with] joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: You turned my wailing into a dance. You untied my sackcloth, and you belted joy around me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reversal arrives in a set of clothes. The speaker had worn sackcloth, a coarse cloth of goat's hair worn tied round the waist by mourners and penitents, and the cord is loosened; then God girds him, ties a belt round him, but this time with joy. The KJV 'put off my sackcloth' hides the Hebrew verb: patach means to open, to untie, as one unties a knot (Rashi compares the unloading of camels in Genesis 24:32; Metzudat Zion, 'untying the knot'). Joy is not a garment laid on from outside but the belt that holds the man together.

The first line turns on two noisy words: the mispad, the professional wailing of a funeral, becomes machol, the circle dance of a feast (Metzudat Zion links it with machol and rikud). The BBE 'sorrow turned to dancing' blunts the funeral. In the ancient world mourning had a sound, and so did celebration: the actor can give the two a single rhythm. Malbim imagines a crowd gathered to lament over a body that suddenly breathes, and who begin to dance. Rashi, quoting the rabbis, reads the whole psalm as the voices of Haman, Esther and Mordecai; leave that for the review.

philological_notes.note: 'My wailing, my lament': the ritual funeral cry; KJV 'mourning' is too quiet.
'Dancing, a round dance': Metzudat Zion derives it from the word for circle dances.
'You loosened, untied': the sense is untying a knot, as Rashi (comparing Gen 24:32) and Metzudat Zion say.
'And you girded me': to tie a belt round the waist, an act of readiness and strength; Ibn Ezra says it is for strengthening.

verses.translation_literal: So that [my] glory may make music to you and not be silent. YHWH my God, for ever I will give thanks to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that my glory, my very self, may sing to you and never fall silent. LORD, my God, for ever I will give you thanks.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason for everything before it. The man was pulled up from the pit, and the wailing and sackcloth are gone. Now the psalm says what the rescue was for: he is alive so that something in him can keep singing. Play it as a vow, not as a flourish. The speaker has stared at the other option: in verse 10 he asked whether dust can thank God. Here he answers by choosing the opposite of dust. The one who sings is not silent.

The word the KJV renders 'my glory' is kavod, and the Hebrew has no 'my'. It is literally 'glory', 'weight', 'honor'. The medieval commentators take it as the self or soul, the part of a person that carries weight (Radak and Meiri on Ps 30:13, with Meiri pointing to Ps 16:9; Metzudat Zion defines it as the soul, the 'glory of the body'). A line from verse 10 stands behind it: dust cannot give thanks, but glory can. The KJV 'my glory' is sound but opaque to a modern ear, which hears vanity or splendor. The verb is also not 'sing praise' in a church sense: zamar is to make music, to play and sing to an instrument, so 'sing praise' softens a verb of strings and voice. The last verb, odeka, is the thanks of public confession, the same root used in verse 5. Note the shift of tense: the first clause is a purpose ('so that it may'), and the second is a flat promise ('I will'). 'For ever' is le'olam, an open horizon rather than a stated length, so 'for ever' is accurate but should not sound like a mystical claim. It means as long as he has breath, and beyond that as long as his name is remembered (Radak: his glory will remain after him). The verse closes the psalm on the divine name and a verb of thanks, a circle back to its opening 'I will exalt you'. The KJV's 'Lord' here replaces YHWH, and that substitution hides the personal name the speaker uses in the very last line.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'weight', hence honor and glory. Here the commentators read it as the soul or self, the person's weightiest part, matching Ps 16:9 where 'my glory' rejoices. It is the subject that will sing, set against the 'dust' of verse 10.

Piel of zamar, 'to make music', with the object 'you' attached. My own reading is that it names singing with instruments, which is why 'make music to you' is closer than 'sing praise'. Metzudat David paraphrases the clause as the soul that sings to you and 'does not fall silent from the song'.
The root dmm is to be still or silent, and in verse 13 it answers the silence of the grave in verse 10. Radak says the glory has no pause or silence at all.
